client: Lately, I’ve been feeling really overwhelmed at my new marketing job. The deadlines are so tight, and I constantly feel like I’m not measuring up to my colleagues who seem so much more experienced and confident. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—I mean, it’s just the nature of the job, right? But the anxiety is starting to get to me.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of self-doubt and pressure in this new role, and it’s understandable to feel overwhelmed when comparing yourself to colleagues who seem more experienced. Therapy can help by exploring how these thoughts impact your emotions and finding ways to manage that anxiety more effectively. Would you like to talk more about specific situations where you feel you’re not measuring up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, there was this meeting last week where I had to present a campaign idea. My manager seemed unimpressed, and one of my colleagues jumped in with suggestions that made mine look amateurish. I felt so embarrassed and stupid afterward. I keep replaying it in my head, wondering if I’m even cut out for this job. Therapy sounds helpful in theory, but I don’t know how it can change the fact that I’m just not as good as they are.
therapist: It sounds like that meeting left a deep mark, and it’s hard to shake the feeling of embarrassment and self-doubt. Replaying it in your head suggests this moment has become a focal point for your fears about not being good enough. Let’s explore what’s underneath those thoughts—do you think there’s a chance you’re being harder on yourself than others are being on you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Maybe I am being too hard on myself, but isn't that normal when you're new? The colleague who corrected me has been there for five years. I just hate feeling like the weak link on the team. Every morning when I walk into the office, my stomach drops because I'm waiting for the next moment where I'll look incompetent.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of pressure to prove yourself, and it’s natural to feel that way when you’re new. But I notice you’re dismissing your own feelings by comparing yourself to someone with much more experience—do you think that’s fair to you? Let’s talk about how we can shift focus from where you think you’re falling short to where you’re actually growing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: You're right that I shouldn't compare myself to someone with five years of experience. But how do I stop? Every time I try to focus on my progress, that awful presentation comes rushing back. I've started avoiding speaking up in meetings now, which isn't helping either.
therapist: It sounds like that presentation has become a kind of mental roadblock, making it hard for you to move forward or see your progress. Avoiding meetings might feel safer in the short term, but I wonder if it’s also keeping you from opportunities to build confidence. Would it help to explore ways to reframe that experience so it doesn’t hold so much power over you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying, but reframing feels easier said than done. That presentation felt like such a public failure, and now I’m scared of making the same mistake. I don’t know how to stop seeing it as proof that I’m not good enough. Every time I try to think positively, it feels forced and fake.
therapist: It makes sense that trying to think positively feels forced when the memory of that presentation is still so vivid and painful. It’s okay to acknowledge that it was a tough moment without letting it define your entire worth or ability. Let’s work on finding small, realistic ways to rebuild your confidence—what’s one thing you could try in your next meeting that feels manageable?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could try just asking one question in the next meeting instead of staying silent the whole time. But even that makes me nervous—what if it's a dumb question and they think I'm not keeping up? I still feel like I need to prove I belong there.
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of asking one question feels risky, as if it could confirm your fears about not belonging. But I wonder if staying silent is also reinforcing that belief—what do you think might happen if you took that small step and asked a question, even if it feels imperfect?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I don't know...maybe they wouldn't think it's a dumb question at all? But after that last presentation, my confidence is so shot that I can't tell what's reasonable anymore. Part of me thinks I should just keep quiet until I have something really impressive to say, but then I'll never get better, will I?
therapist: It sounds like you’re caught between wanting to improve and feeling too unsure to take even small steps forward. But it’s insightful of you to notice that staying quiet might hold you back from getting better. What would it feel like to see asking a question not as a test of your worth, but as a way to learn and grow?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I never thought about questions being for learning instead of proving myself. But honestly, it still feels terrifying—what if I ask something and it turns out I should already know the answer? My mind keeps telling me everyone will judge me for not being as sharp as they are.
therapist: Your voice sounds really strained as you describe this fear—it’s clear how much weight you’re carrying with this worry about being judged. I wonder if there’s a part of you that feels like you need to already know everything, even though you’re new to this role. What would it feel like to give yourself permission to not have all the answers right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: That actually makes me tear up a little. I *do* feel like I need to know everything already, and it's exhausting. But if I give myself permission not to know...wouldn't that make me slack off? I'm scared if I lower my standards at all, I'll completely fail.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a lot of fear tied to the idea of lowering your standards—like it might mean giving up or failing altogether. But giving yourself permission to not know everything doesn’t mean you’re slacking off; it means you’re allowing yourself to grow and learn at your own pace. How does that idea feel to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: It feels...scary but also kind of relieving. Like maybe I’ve been holding myself to an impossible standard, and it’s okay to admit that. But I’m still worried that if I ease up, I’ll fall behind even more. I don’t want to end up being the person everyone thinks isn’t pulling their weight.
therapist: It sounds like there’s a mix of relief and fear as you start to consider easing the pressure on yourself—relief because you’re acknowledging how impossible those standards feel, but fear that letting go might mean falling behind. What would it look like to find a balance where you’re still striving but not holding yourself to perfection?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
